new_statements.quote: As a guide to proper pronunciation, accent marks are used to indicate which syllable or syllables are to be stressed. An acute accent ( ' ) is used to mark the strongest stress in the word while the circumflex accent ( ^ ) is used when the final syllable is stressed and at the same time has a glottal stop.
new_statements.citation: Meman, Paz B. 1990. Viracnon Language Packet. Manila: Peace Corps (ERIC ED402759). Glossary section (developed by Yolanda Sena), Explanatory Notes.
new_statements.locator: Glossary, Explanatory Notes, printed p. 142 (PDF p. 96 of the archive.org scan micro_IA41153411_0770); lexically marked glossary entries begin printed p. 143 (PDF p. 97)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (275 pp, archive.org micro_IA41153411_0770, ERIC ED402759). PDF p. 96 = printed p. 142 "EXPLANATORY NOTES" (glossary front matter). The page image reads exactly: "As a guide to proper pronunciation, accent marks are used to indicate which syllable or syllables are to be stressed. / An acute accent ( ') is used to mark the strongest stress in the word while the circumflex accent ( ^) is used when the final syllable is stressed and at the same time has a glottal stop." The extracted text layer renders the circumflex as a curly quote, but the image shows ^ as quoted. Quote is verbatim. Surrounding section: abbreviation key and a note that the appendix lists verb roots; nothing else on p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source gives no positional rule: stress placement is treated as a property of each word that must be marked in the glossary. The marked entries on the first glossary page show both penultimate stress (ága 'morning', áki 'child', áldaw 'day', ámo 'nickname', áni 'harvest', abokádo, Agósto, akásya, Amérika) and final stress (abaká, abó 'ash', abohón 'gray', agóm 'spouse', akó 'I', amá 'father', anó 'what', anóm 'six', apát 'four', aparadór). This is consistent with the lexically contrastive (penult vs. ultima) stress known for the Bikol subgroup, but Meman does not state contrastiveness explicitly; the reading is inferred from the marking practice.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The note speaks of the acute marking 'the strongest stress in the word' and of 'syllable or syllables' being stressed, which implies more than one stressed syllable can be marked, but no entry with two marks was checked and no secondary-stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Some function words are left unmarked (e.g., kaya (PA) 'expression for uncertainty', printed p. 152, next to kayá (C) 'that's why'; ko 'by me; my'), which suggests clitic particles carry no marked stress, but the source does not say so.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a learner's glossary (mostly bare roots and some affixed verb forms). Word-final stress plus glottal stop gets a separate circumflex mark. Nothing on phrase-level accent, and nothing in the Grammar Notes or the workbook beyond an exercise asking learners to 'mark syllable stress as needed' (printed p. 175, PDF p. 129).
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the variety "Viracnon" / "Bikol-Viracnon" (the speech of Virac, Catanduanes), which is exactly Glottolog sout2912 / ISO bln (Southern Catanduanes Bikol). Lobel 2013 groups it under Coastal Bikol; no separate glottocode needed.

sources.locator: Glossary, Explanatory Notes, printed p. 142 (PDF p. 96 of the archive.org scan micro_IA41153411_0770); lexically marked glossary entries begin printed p. 143 (PDF p. 97)
sources.note: No phonology chapter. Only the glossary's Explanatory Notes (printed p. 142) state that accent marks indicate which syllable(s) are stressed, acute = strongest stress, circumflex = final stress plus glottal stop; every glossary entry is individually marked and both penult and final stress occur (p. 143). Grammar Notes and Phrase Book say nothing about stress; the workbook has one 'mark syllable stress' exercise (p. 175).

sources.note: Nothing specific to Southern Catanduanes / Virac Bikol (only two passing mentions of Northern Catanduanes Bikol vowel reflexes, pp. 234 and 252). Footnote 3, p. 287 (PDF p. 301): 'It is not at all uncommon for one or more members of a Philippine subgroup to have lost contrastive stress while others retain it, as this is exactly what has happened both in the Bikol subgroup (Lobel 2003) and the Cordilleran subgroup (Zorc 1979).' Section 8.2.9 'Contrastive Accent' (p. 259) concerns Manide and Inagta Alabat, not Bikol.
